title: Talking with Morton: his records, Simeon and his left hand
summary: Morton's remembered records under other names, Simeon, flutter tonguing, and his piano style as orchestra.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: He said, here's a man who knows all my pieces and all. He was very pleased. So after talking a while, he said he'd made so many records he couldn't remember all of them. He mentioned, at that time, we didn't know all of his records either and we still probably don't. But he mentioned he'd made some under other names and all too. But that might have been something like those Vocalions. He didn't have his name on all of those. Anyway, when the subject of Simeon came up and also about Earl Hines, that Simeon was working with Hines, he was disgusted that Hines, I mean that Simeon had to work with somebody like Hines, which might have been a little bit of jealousy, but still at one time he was considered a lot higher than Hines, I guess, back in the early Chicago days. So he thought that was a shame that he had to work with a guy like Hines. And he mentioned that Simeon was his favorite clarinetist. And he mentioned he'd also recorded with the Bach K. At that time we didn't know, I don't believe that he'd ever recorded with Bach K. So he went over his jukebox and put a nickel in and played a record, one of the New Orleans Bump, I think. It has some funny flutter tonguing in there on clarinet, which they don't do anymore. Incidentally, even George Lewis used to do it in New York around 1942. Five and Six. You never hear George do anything like that here, but do that same rough growling and flutter tonguing, which is, hardly ever anybody does it here, but Bach K. was doing it on that record all the way through one chorus. We never could find out any records that Jellie had made with Jimmy Noon, although he said he had made them. When I asked him which ones, he said Grandpa Spells, I believe. But we never could find them. But I'll copy some of these notes sometime, which I remember when I asked Jellie to play, he started talking about his left hand and all. He said players today don't have a left hand, of course, which is true if you take some of the fellows that just play up in the treble, with somebody where they're heard more. They don't do it. He probably has a pretty good left hand at that. But I mean, some of them got a style just playing up high where they're heard more and they don't do anything with the bass. But he was very proud of his left hand and always made a point of that. So I mentioned...
I don't know any other pianists in the... Do you?

No. Of course, he explains even, I think, on the Library of Congress that the piano is sort of a substitute for orchestra to a whole band and he seemed to... That may not really be a characteristic piano style to try to imitate. I don't think he was necessarily trying to imitate a piano but at least he was filling in everything, playing all the different parts which the piano can do. He told a little bit about the records he made with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. I think that's been pretty well covered in different magazine articles.
